lessons.title: Full Stack Mental Model
lessons.body:
Phase 00

How Modern Full-
Stack Applications
Work
A visual mental model for browsers, frontend
rendering, APIs, business logic, persistence,
authentication and state ownership.

Book 1 · Full-stack mental model
Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented

Contents
1. A request is a journey                           7. The API boundary

2. Browser responsibilities                         8. State ownership

3. Frontend responsibilities                        9. Failure paths

4. Backend responsibilities                       10. The complete request lifecycle

5. Database responsibilities                      11. Knowledge checks

6. Authentication vs authorization

Phase 00 | Page 2 of 10

A request is a journey through
responsibilities
When a user clicks Create Task, no single framework “does the feature.” Multiple layers cooperate.
Becoming a full-stack developer means understanding that journey well enough to diagnose it when
something goes wrong.

Browser

Next.js frontend

HTTP API request

NestJS controller + service

Prisma data access

Supabase PostgreSQL

Figure 1 - Core application request path - This is the central diagram we will repeatedly expand throughout the
course.

Layer 1: the browser

The browser renders HTML and CSS, runs client-side JavaScript, stores limited client state, sends
network requests, receives responses, enforces web security rules such as CORS, and reports failures
in developer tools. It does not decide authoritative business rules just because it can run code.

Layer 2: Next.js

Next.js is the presentation application. It owns routes, pages, layouts, rendering choices, UI
composition, navigation and interaction. Later it also coordinates client-side server state through
TanStack Query. The course deliberately prevents Next.js from becoming a second backend full of
duplicated business rules.

Phase 00 | Page 3 of 10

Layer 3: HTTP

HTTP is the contract boundary between independently running applications. A request carries a
method, URL, headers and optional body. A response carries a status code, headers and optional
body. This boundary is valuable because the frontend and backend can evolve independently as long
as they honor the contract.

Method                            Path                      Headers                      Body
POST                            /tasks                Auth, Content-Type                JSON

NestJS route receives the request

Figure 2 - HTTP request anatomy - The API boundary is explicit; it is not a function call disguised as networking.

Layer 4: NestJS + Fastify

NestJS provides the application architecture for controllers, providers, dependency injection, guards,
interceptors and modules. Fastify is the HTTP platform underneath NestJS in this course. Controllers
translate HTTP into application calls; services own business behavior.

Phase 00 | Page 4 of 10

HTTP request

Controller

Validation / auth boundary

Service business logic

PrismaService

Database

Figure 3 - Backend responsibility chain - Keep controllers thin enough that business rules remain reusable and
testable.

ASP.NET CORE BRIDGE

If you know ASP.NET Core: a Nest controller is conceptually similar to a controller, providers/
services use dependency injection, guards/interceptors overlap with filter/middleware concerns,
and PrismaService loosely occupies the “database access gateway” role that DbContext often
plays. The mapping is useful, but the frameworks are not identical.

Layer 5: Prisma

Prisma is not PostgreSQL. It is the application-facing ORM/data-access layer. It turns model
definitions into typed database operations and manages schema changes through migrations. In our
architecture, Prisma stays behind NestJS so browser code never receives database credentials.

Layer 6: PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL is authoritative persistent storage for application data: users, memberships, projects,
tasks, comments, audit history and other relational records. Supabase hosts PostgreSQL for the
course, but the relational concepts remain standard PostgreSQL concepts.

Phase 00 | Page 5 of 10

Authentication is not authorization

Authentication answers “who are you?” Authorization answers “are you allowed to perform this
action on this resource?” Those questions happen at different points and should remain conceptually
separate.

User signs in

Supabase Auth

Access token (JWT)

Next.js sends Bearer token

NestJS validates token

Service receives trusted identity

Figure 4 - Future authentication flow - Authentication establishes a trustworthy identity before business logic
evaluates permissions.

Later, authorization adds another decision:

Phase 00 | Page 6 of 10

Verified user

Requested action

Membership / role / ownership check

Allowed?

Execute business operation

Figure 5 - Authorization decision - A valid identity is necessary but not sufficient; permissions and resource ownership
still matter.

State ownership

Many frontend applications become difficult because every kind of state is placed in one global store.
The course teaches state by ownership instead.

Server-owned state                                                 Client-owned state

TanStack Query                                                Local / URL / Form state
tasks · projects · users · API results                             dialogs · filters · inputs · navigation

Persistent truth                                                  Domain behavior

PostgreSQL                                                Services / optional stores
authoritative business data                                        rules and interaction logic

Figure 6 - State ownership map - Different categories of state deserve different tools and lifecycles.

Phase 00 | Page 7 of 10

Failure paths are part of the architecture

A professional mental model includes failure. Network requests time out. Validation rejects input.
Authentication expires. Authorization denies access. Database constraints conflict. Bugs throw
exceptions. The goal is not to pretend failures are rare; the goal is to know which layer should detect,
translate, log and present them.

Database                    Prisma                     Service                    HTTP
constraint                   error                     decision                    409

UI message
“Already exists”

Figure 7 - Failure translation - Errors should become more meaningful as they travel toward the user.

Phase 00 | Page 8 of 10

The full lifecycle

User interaction

React / Next.js UI

TanStack Query or API client

HTTP + JWT

NestJS controller

Guard / validation

Service

Prisma

PostgreSQL

Response + cache update

UI re-renders

Figure 8 - Complete vertical slice - This is the mental model you should be able to narrate from memory by the end of
Phase 00.

Knowledge checks

1. Why should Next.js not receive a PostgreSQL password?
2. What responsibility would be lost if all business logic lived in controllers?
3. What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

Phase 00 | Page 9 of 10

4. Where does durable business data live?
5. Why is HTTP useful even when frontend and backend are in one monorepo?
6. Give one example of server state and one example of local UI state.

YOU ARE READY WHEN

You can narrate the request path without memorizing framework slogans: user → UI → HTTP →
controller → service → Prisma → PostgreSQL → response → UI.

Phase 00 | Page 10 of 10

objectives: Explain Full Stack Mental Model in terms of concrete inputs, ownership, outputs, and evidence.
Implement or reproduce the smallest TaskFlow slice that demonstrates this architecture concept.
Diagnose one representative architecture failure using observable evidence instead of trial-and-error.
workshop.why: Full Stack Mental Model matters because it changes a real boundary in TaskFlow. The goal is to understand the inputs, owner, observable output, and failure modes before adding more abstraction.
steps: Restate the goal of “Full Stack Mental Model” as one observable behavior. Write the success signal before touching code.
Trace the boundary map: User intent → UI boundary → API contract → business rule → persistence → observable result. Mark the one boundary this lesson changes.
Inspect the current repository state and record the exact files, route, table, or runtime involved. Avoid creating an abstraction before you can name the existing owner.
Implement the smallest vertical slice. Add one coherent change, run the narrowest verification command, and read the output before continuing.

Connect the slice to TaskFlow’s phase artifact: A one-page architecture map plus an ADR-style note describing the responsibilities of Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, PostgreSQL/Supabase, and supporting infrastructure.. Verify behavior from the outside as a user or API client would.
Create one controlled failure that is safe to reproduce. Predict the symptom first, capture evidence, locate the earliest broken boundary, then fix only that cause.
Close the reference and rebuild or explain the core change from memory. Record what you would monitor or test before trusting the same change in production.

example.caption: Boundary trace
example.code: Input -> owner -> transformation -> observable output -> failure evidence

verify: Run the narrowest relevant command or request and require a clean exit/status.
Inspect the boundary-specific evidence: terminal output, Network panel, database row/query plan, test report, container health, or deployment logs.
Repeat the behavior once after the change so a one-off cached or stale result cannot masquerade as success.
breakIt: Putting business rules in React components
Change one assumption in the architecture example—identity, input, configuration, ordering, connectivity, or state—and predict the exact symptom before running it.

troubleshooting.symptom: Expected result does not appear
troubleshooting.investigation: Return to the nearest observable boundary: input, network, process log, database, or rendered UI. Compare actual evidence with the predicted path.

troubleshooting.symptom: A shortcut appears to fix it
troubleshooting.investigation: Change one variable at a time and reproduce the original failure after the fix; otherwise you have correlation, not diagnosis.

workshop.challenge: Without copying the final source, create a second small scenario that applies “Full Stack Mental Model” to a different TaskFlow resource or input. Write the acceptance criteria first, implement it, and provide the evidence that each criterion is satisfied.
review: What problem does Full Stack Mental Model solve in TaskFlow, and what would be observably wrong without it?
Which part of the architecture boundary owns the decision, and which neighboring layer must not own it?
What evidence proves the happy path instead of merely suggesting it worked?
Name one realistic failure or abuse case and the first place you would inspect.
If requirements doubled tomorrow, which part of this design should stay stable and which part is allowed to change?

Phase 00

TaskFlow Production
System Blueprint
The product we will grow throughout the course -
scope, domain model, vertical slices, security
boundaries and final production architecture.

Book 2 · Capstone system blueprint
Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented

Contents
1. Why TaskFlow                          7. Security model preview

2. Product capabilities                  8. Frontend information architecture

3. Domain vocabulary                     9. Operational capabilities

4. Growth stages                       10. What is intentionally excluded early

5. Core data model                     11. Enterprise transfer

6. API surface preview

Phase 00 | Page 2 of 7

Why TaskFlow instead of a giant
enterprise domain on day one?
The project must be complex enough to teach production engineering, but simple enough that
architecture remains visible. TaskFlow starts with a personal Todo feature, then grows into a
workspace-based collaboration system. Each expansion introduces one new class of engineering
problem.

Product capabilities at graduation

Identity                                                   Organizations
Signup, login, logout, session refresh,                    Workspaces, membership, invitations, roles
protected routes and profile basics.                       and ownership.

Projects                                                   Tasks
Project lifecycle, status, metadata and                    Create, assign, prioritize, filter, paginate,
membership-aware access.                                   complete and archive.

Collaboration                                              Operations
Comments, activity history, notifications and              Audit logs, testing, structured logs, health
carefully selected realtime.                               checks, CI/CD and deployment.

Domain vocabulary

Concept      Meaning in TaskFlow                                      Why it matters architecturally

User         Authenticated identity represented by Supabase           Identity must be trusted from a verified token,
Auth plus application profile data.                      not a browser-supplied userId.

Workspace    Tenant/team boundary containing projects and             Introduces multi-tenant authorization.
members.

Membership   Relationship between a user and workspace with           Introduces many-to-many modeling and RBAC.
a role.

Project      Container for collaborative work.                        Introduces parent-child resource ownership.

Phase 00 | Page 3 of 7

Task           Unit of work with status, priority and                    Exercises CRUD, validation, filtering and
assignment.                                               optimistic updates.

Activity       Immutable description of important domain                 Introduces audit/history thinking.
events.

User                       Membership                              Workspace

Project

Comment / Activity                                Task

Figure 1 - Domain relationship preview - This is a conceptual map, not yet a final database schema.

Growth stages

We do not create the final schema on day one. The product grows in vertical slices so the learner can
see cause and effect.

Phase 00 | Page 4 of 7

Health check

Personal Todo CRUD

Validated Todo API

Authenticated personal Todos

Workspace membership

Projects + collaborative Tasks

Permissions + activity

Production capabilities

Figure 2 - Vertical-slice growth - Each stage should produce a usable, testable application state.

API surface preview

GET    /health
GET    /todos
POST   /todos
PATCH /todos/:id
DELETE /todos/:id

# Later
GET     /workspaces
POST    /workspaces
GET     /workspaces/:workspaceId/projects
POST    /projects/:projectId/tasks
PATCH /tasks/:taskId
POST    /tasks/:taskId/comments

THE CONTRACT GROWS WITH THE DOMAIN

We start with resource-oriented REST endpoints because they keep the HTTP boundary visible.
More advanced patterns are introduced only if a concrete problem appears.

Phase 00 | Page 5 of 7

Security boundary preview

Browser signs in

Supabase Auth issues session

Next.js attaches access token

NestJS verifies token

Membership/ownership checked

Authorized service operation

Figure 3 - Trusted identity path - Never use a raw browser-supplied user id as proof of identity.

Frontend information architecture

TaskFlow App Shell

Dashboard                    Projects                   My Tasks               Workspace Settings

Project Detail                Task Detail

Figure 4 - Future application navigation - A practical shell that will exercise layouts, routing, forms, tables and
responsive UI.

Phase 00 | Page 6 of 7

Operational capabilities we will eventually add

• Structured logging and request correlation.
• Health/readiness endpoints.
• Environment separation.
• Database migrations as a controlled deployment step.
• Unit and integration tests for business behavior.
• Playwright end-to-end flows.
• CI quality gates.
• Production deployment and rollback thinking.

What is intentionally excluded early

Microservices, Kubernetes, Kafka, CQRS, event sourcing, GraphQL, distributed caches and complex
domain-driven architecture are not prerequisites for learning to build a high-quality production
application. They can be valuable in the right system, but adding them before the application has
demonstrated the problem they solve makes the architecture harder to understand.

Enterprise transfer

TaskFlow concept          HRIS analogue                          Procurement analogue

Workspace                 Company / business unit                Organization / department

Membership + role         Employee + role/position               Requester / approver authority

Project                   Leave cycle / HR process               Procurement request / sourcing event

Task status               Workflow state                         Approval / PO / receiving state

Activity log              HR audit history                       Procurement audit trail

DESIGN PRINCIPLE

The course teaches patterns through TaskFlow, but every architecture explanation asks how the
same responsibility would appear in a larger business system.

Phase 00

2026 Locked
Technology & Version
Manifest
A stable course baseline that prevents silent major-
version drift and makes every command, file and
explanation internally consistent.

Book 3 · Technology decisions and upgrade policy
Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented

Contents
1. Why version locks matter                  7. TypeScript

2. Primary locked baseline                   8. Frontend libraries

3. Why Node 24 LTS                           9. Testing and styling

4. Next.js + React                         10. Version verification commands

5. NestJS + Fastify                        11. Upgrade policy

6. Prisma policy                           12. Source notes

Phase 00 | Page 2 of 6

Why version locks matter in a long
course
Framework documentation changes quickly. A command that is correct for one major version may be
wrong for another. The course therefore separates current ecosystem awareness from course
reproducibility. We research current stable releases at course start, choose the baseline, record it,
then stop silently upgrading.

CRITICAL COURSE RULE

A newer version appearing during the course is a note, not permission to rewrite completed
phases. Upgrades are separate engineering exercises with their own migration plan.

Form                                 begins

baseline                       Tailwind comes as an applied UI track.

Playwright          1.63.0           Lock when E2E phase            Cross-browser end-to-end testing baseline.
begins

Node.js: prefer LTS for a production learning
baseline

Node 26 is the Current release line, while Node 24 is LTS. Production applications should generally
target an LTS line rather than using Current merely because the number is larger. The course locks
Node 24.21.0 so tooling and native dependencies are reproducible.

Node 26                             Node 24                                Course
Current                               LTS                                Node 24.21.0

Figure 1 - Release choice is not “largest version wins” - Course stability prefers an LTS runtime while still
documenting what Current means.

Next.js + React

Next.js 16.3 is the Active LTS line. The course baseline uses the patched 16.3.3 release rather than
an older vulnerable 16.x patch. React 19.3.0 is the current stable React release and is paired with the
Next.js 16.3 course line.

Phase 00 | Page 4 of 6

NestJS + Fastify

NestJS 12.0.3 is paired with Fastify 5.12.5. Fastify 6 is alpha at the course lock date, so it is
intentionally excluded. This is a recurring course lesson: production engineering values maturity and
compatibility over novelty.

Prisma: the deliberate exception

Prisma 8 is in release-candidate status in September 2026 and changes the workflow substantially.
The supplied course specification requires Prisma 7.9.1. That is a sensible educational constraint:
Prisma 7 remains supported, and locking 7.9.1 prevents a long-running course from mixing Prisma 7
commands with Prisma 8 behavior.

HARD LOCK

Every Prisma command in this course must be version-consistent with 7.9.1. If a later phase
needs an upgrade, the upgrade is taught as a migration project rather than performed silently.

Verification commands

# Run from the appropriate project/workspace directory
node -v
pnpm -v
pnpm exec tsc -v
pnpm exec next --version
pnpm exec nest --version
pnpm exec prisma version

# Package versions can also be inspected from package.json / pnpm-lock.yaml

Course dependency policy

1. Pin majors and important patch versions deliberately.
2. Commit the lockfile.
3. Never copy a command from documentation without checking the documentation version.
4. Security patches receive explicit review; they are not ignored merely because versions are
locked.
5. Major upgrades happen between milestones, with tests green before and after.

Source notes checked September 17, 2026

• Node.js Releases: nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases and release blog.

Phase 00 | Page 5 of 6

• Next.js Blog: Next.js 16.3 and August 2026 security release.
• React Blog: React 19.3, September 9, 2026.
• NestJS GitHub releases: v12.0.3, September 15, 2026; Nest CLI 12.0.3.
• Fastify npm: 5.12.5 stable; 6.0.0 alpha excluded.
• TypeScript GitHub releases: 7.0.2.
• Prisma v7 docs and release-status page; course hard lock is 7.9.1.
• pnpm npm/GitHub release: 12.4.2.
• Package registries checked for React Hook Form, Zod, TanStack Query, Supabase JS, Tailwind CSS and Playwright.

WHAT TO REMEMBER

The manifest is a contract. It exists so a lesson written in Phase 08 still makes sense when you
are in Phase 30.

lessons.title: Engineering Workflow
lessons.body:
Phase 00

Engineering Workflow,
Windows First
How professional developers move from
requirement to branch, code, verification,
debugging, review and deployable change.

Book 4 · Workflow, discipline and development habits
Course baseline: September 17, 2026 · Windows-first · Project-driven · Production-oriented

Contents
1. The engineering loop                            7. Environment variables and secrets

2. Windows and PowerShell conventions              8. Git workflow

3. Repository discipline                           9. Definition of done

4. Working-directory awareness                   10. Documentation habits

5. Small verified changes                        11. AI-assisted development rules

6. Debugging by layer

Phase 00 | Page 2 of 6

The engineering loop matters more
than typing speed
requirement, locate the responsible layer, make the smallest coherent change, verify behavior, and
preserve a clean history.

Requirement / bug report

Locate responsibility

Plan smallest vertical change

Implement

Run checks

Inspect runtime behavior

Commit coherent change

Figure 1 - Professional change loop - This loop is repeated from the first health endpoint to production deployment.

Windows-first command discipline

The course uses ordinary Windows PowerShell as the primary shell. Every command will say where it
runs. Paths containing spaces are quoted. Bash-only syntax is never silently mixed into PowerShell
instructions.

cd "C:\Projects\TaskFlow\apps\api"
Get-Location
pnpm run start:dev

Phase 00 | Page 3 of 6

THE WORKING DIRECTORY IS PART OF THE COMMAND

A correct command executed from the wrong workspace can produce a misleading package,
script or configuration error. Always include location in your debugging model.

User-profile tooling instead of unnecessary admin
rights

On restricted Windows machines, global package setup should prefer user-owned locations rather
than assuming Administrator privileges. The course will document permission failures such as
Corepack attempting writes under C:\Program Files\nodejs , then teach a user-profile installation
strategy when appropriate.

Repository discipline

• One responsibility per new file.
• No “utils” dumping ground when a specific module owns the behavior.
• Do not create a package simply because a packages/ directory exists.
• Commit the lockfile.
• Keep secrets out of Git.
• Run lint/typecheck/tests/build at meaningful checkpoints.

taskflow/ workspace

apps/web                                                   apps/api
Next.js                                                NestJS + Fastify

packages/*
only when justified

Figure 2 - Repository responsibility map - The monorepo is a container for independently owned applications and later
shared packages.

Phase 00 | Page 4 of 6

Debugging by layer

When an error appears, avoid replacing whole files. First determine which layer can actually produce
the observed symptom.

Symptom                         First layer to inspect                  Example evidence

Button does nothing             Browser/UI                              Console, event handler, disabled state.

Request blocked before API      Browser/network                         DevTools Network, CORS message.

404/405                         HTTP/controller routing                 Method/path mismatch.

401/403                         Authentication/authorization            Token/guard/permission logs.

400/422                         Validation boundary                     DTO/schema error details.

409                             Business rule/database constraint       Unique conflict or domain rule.

500                             Backend runtime/data access             Server logs and stack trace.

Reproduce reliably

Inspect browser console/network

Confirm HTTP route and status

Inspect server log/request id

Inspect service decision

Inspect database query/constraint

Environment variables and secrets

Configuration enters the course when a layer first needs it. Secrets never appear in screenshots,
example repositories or PDF source snippets. Public browser variables and server-only secrets are
treated differently.

Phase 00 | Page 5 of 6

# Example documentation only
DATABASE_URL="postgresql://..."
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL="http://localhost:4000"

Git workflow for learning and real projects

1. Start from a known-green main branch.
2. Create a focused branch for a coherent change.
3. Make small, verifiable commits.
4. Keep generated artifacts and secrets out of commits unless intentionally versioned.
5. Before merge: lint, typecheck, tests and production build.
6. Review the diff for accidental files and architecture drift.

Definition of done

□ Requirement is satisfied.
□ Expected behavior was manually verified.
□ Error/failure path is understood.
□ Lint passes.
□ Typecheck passes.
□ Relevant tests pass.
□ Production build passes when applicable.
□ No secret or debug artifact leaked.
□ Architecture documentation still matches reality.

AI-assisted development rules

AI can accelerate explanation, search, refactoring and test design, but it should not erase your
mental model. The course treats AI like a pair programmer: it may propose changes, but you should
be able to explain what layer changed, why the change is correct, and how you verified it.

RULE FOR THIS COURSE

Never accept a large generated patch as “correct” because it compiles. Read the diff, identify
the responsibility of every new file, and verify the behavior at the boundary that matters.

Phase 00

Exercises, Knowledge
Checks & Phase Exit
Turn the diagrams into working mental models
before Phase 01 introduces tools and commands.

Book 6 · Active learning and assessment

Phase 00 | Page 2 of 7

Phase 00 is complete only when you
can reason without the diagram
This book converts passive reading into active recall. Do the exercises before reading the answer
guide. The goal is not perfect wording; the goal is correct ownership and causal reasoning.

Warm-up questions

1. What problem does a backend API solve that a purely browser-based application cannot safely
solve?
2. Why is Prisma not the database?
3. Why does a valid JWT not automatically mean a user may edit every task?
4. What is the value of keeping Next.js and NestJS independent even inside one repository?
5. Why might Node 24 LTS be a better course runtime than Node 26 Current?
6. Why are major-version upgrades treated as separate projects?

Architecture classification

For each responsibility, write the primary owning layer: browser/Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, PostgreSQL,
Supabase Auth, TanStack Query, or CI/CD.

1. Upgrade immediately because newer is always better.

The browser is not a trusted security boundary. The backend must verify the token, establish the

Guided Build Lab — Phase 00: Full-Stack Architecture & Orientation

Purpose
Explain the complete TaskFlow request path and identify which layer owns presentation, transport, business rules, persistence, identity, and operations.

Deliverable
A one-page architecture map plus an ADR-style note describing the responsibilities of Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, PostgreSQL/Supabase, and supporting infrastructure.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
Browser interaction -> Next.js presentation boundary -> HTTP request -> NestJS controller/guard -> Service/business rules -> Prisma persistence -> PostgreSQL -> HTTP response -> UI update

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Draw TaskFlow as boxes and arrows before opening an IDE.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Label every arrow with what crosses it: props, HTTP JSON, verified identity, Prisma calls, SQL results.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. Step 3 — Write one responsibility and one non-responsibility for each layer.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 4 — Trace create-task from click to database commit and back to the screen.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Step 6 — Record the architecture decisions that should remain stable through later phases.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 00: Full-Stack Architecture & Orientation

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
Browser interaction -> Next.js presentation boundary -> HTTP request -> NestJS controller/guard -> Service/business rules -> Prisma persistence -> PostgreSQL -> HTTP response -> UI update

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Putting business rules in React components
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Letting controllers call the database directly everywhere
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Treating Supabase as one undifferentiated magic backend
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Choosing infrastructure before defining responsibilities
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.summary:
Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 00 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?
lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Full-Stack Architecture & Orientation

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 00 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Explain the complete TaskFlow request path and identify which layer owns presentation, transport, business rules, persistence, identity, and operations.

Required artifact
A one-page architecture map plus an ADR-style note describing the responsibilities of Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, PostgreSQL/Supabase, and supporting infrastructure.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can trace a request without skipping a layer.
• Can explain why the API owns rules.
• Can distinguish authentication from authorization.
• Can name which concerns are deployment concerns rather than business logic.

Independent build sequence
1. Draw TaskFlow as boxes and arrows before opening an IDE.
2. Label every arrow with what crosses it: props, HTTP JSON, verified identity, Prisma calls, SQL results.
3. Write one responsibility and one non-responsibility for each layer.
4. Trace create-task from click to database commit and back to the screen.
5. Trace one failure: invalid input, missing authentication, forbidden action, database outage.
6. Record the architecture decisions that should remain stable through later phases.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.title: Mastery Capstone Lab
lessons.summary: Integrate Phase 00 without following a transcript.
lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 00: Full-Stack Architecture & Orientation. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
A one-page architecture map plus an ADR-style note describing the responsibilities of Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, PostgreSQL/Supabase, and supporting infrastructure.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

Produce a reproducible evidence packet for success and failure.
Defend the architecture and identify one improvement without overengineering.
workshop.why: A guided lesson proves you can follow. A capstone proves you can transfer the model to a requirement with fewer cues.

Label every arrow with what crosses it: props, HTTP JSON, verified identity, Prisma calls, SQL results.
Write one responsibility and one non-responsibility for each layer.
Trace create-task from click to database commit and back to the screen.
Trace one failure: invalid input, missing authentication, forbidden action, database outage.
Record the architecture decisions that should remain stable through later phases.
